title: Gujrat and annexation, 1849
hookLine: the last battle is lost, the soldiers lay down their arms, and the Punjab is annexed

cards: A line of soldiers comes forward, one by one, and lays its weapons on a pile: swords, matchlocks, shields. These are men of the Khalsa army, and the war is over. A story is told about that day.
An old soldier, setting down his arms, says quietly that today Ranjit Singh has died. The Maharaja was long dead. But the kingdom he built was ending in front of them.

teach.b: Gujrat here is a town in the Punjab, not the Indian state with a similar name. After Chillianwala, the British waited for more troops, and above all more heavy guns.
At Gujrat they used them: a long, heavy bombardment came before the infantry moved, and this time the Sikh line broke. The British pursued the retreating army.
Its leaders, Sher Singh Attariwala and his father Chattar Singh, gave themselves up, and the soldiers handed over their arms. That's where the old soldier's story is set.
It may be remembered more than recorded, but Sikhs keep telling it because it says what the day meant. Lord Dalhousie did not restore the court at Lahore.

He declared the Punjab part of British India. The boy Maharaja, Duleep Singh, still a child, was made to put his name to terms that gave up his kingdom and his claims to it. The flag over the fort at Lahore was changed.
Near the close of the Guru Granth Sahib, in his saloks, Guru Tegh Bahadur describes a person whose strength has gone, who is bound and can find no way out.

teach.h: BOUND, AND THEN THE VERSE TURNS.
teach.b: In the next breath the verse turns: strength returns, the bonds fall away, and everything is in the Lord's hands. The Guru doesn't pretend the binding isn't real. He just doesn't stop the verse there.
A kingdom did end at Gujrat, and the old soldier's story doesn't hide it.

how: Sikh histories mark the defeat at Gujrat and the annexation that followed as the end of the Sikh kingdom of the Punjab, and the story of the soldiers laying down their arms is still told at gatherings about that history.

o: bonds, being tied up with no way to get free
a family line handed down to a son
a vow of loyalty made to a new ruler

games.q: the end of a kingdom — tap the pairs.

s: Gujrat is the Indian state of Gujarat
it's a town in the Punjab; the names are only similar.
after the war the court at Lahore was restored
Dalhousie declared the Punjab part of British India.
the story of the old soldier says today Ranjit Singh has died
the kingdom he built was ending in front of them.

games.q: you're a soldier of the Khalsa army. the war is lost, and your leaders have given themselves up. what happens, as the story is told?
o: you keep fighting in the hills.
you lay down your arms, and an old soldier says today Ranjit Singh has died.
you join the British army that day.
games.why: the soldiers handed over their arms; the old soldier's words are remembered because they say what the day meant.

practice: Let your shoulders drop and bring to mind one thing in your life that is over and won't come back: a school you left, a team you played on, a routine you shared with someone, a version of yourself.
Don't argue with it or dress it up; notice where you feel it in your body, and breathe into that place, slowly, three or four times. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you breathe out.

wordCard.voice: Bandhan, bonds. Guru Tegh Bahadur's salok speaks of being bound, and then of the bonds falling away, as the last battle was lost to the big guns and the Punjab declared part of British India. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the kingdom ended. Bound, and then the bonds fall away. Nine hundred thirty-nine days, and counting.
